newsitem.title: FRANCE: French union fears Jospin to swing to austerity.
newsitem.headline: French union fears Jospin to swing to austerity.

text.p: A French trade union leader said on Saturday he feared the Socialist-led government would swing to austerity to qualify for a single European currency and warned he would "mobilise troops" in protest if it did.

"The prime minister has not yet spoken of balancing public spending. He will be obliged to do so," said Marc Blondel, head of the independent Force Ouvriere (FO) union. "The consequences could well be the start of a bit of austerity in September".
"We would not accept it and I would mobilise my troops," Blondel told Europe 1 radio. FO is France's third largest union.

Blondel said he feared new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin would drop promises that he would not impose further austerity to qualify for the euro currency from 1999 after a review of public finances was completed in mid-July.

Blondel said he reckoned the audit would show France's budget deficit for 1997 was at about 3.7 or 3.8 percent of gross domestic product, above the three percent that is a criterion for qualifying for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

He said Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn already "very well knows" the state of public finances and that governments did not order audits to conclude with praise for the economic management of previous administrations.

Jospin said in a keynote policy speech on Thursday that France was committed to the euro currency but did not spell out how he would reconcile that promise with the pledge of no extra austerity if the audit showed France's was above the budget deficit hurdle.

Blondel said the FO union would be "neither hostile nor servile" to the government that came to power after an upset parliamentary election victory on June 1, an attitude FO adopted towards the previous centre-right government.
He expressed renewed regret that Jospin planned to raise the minimum wage by just four percent, against a 6.2 percent hike favoured by FO.

FO and the Communist-led CGT union led a crippling 24-day wave of public sector strikes in late 1995 against the former government of prime minister Alain Juppe, a close ally of conservative President Jacques Chirac.
